source: Laban, Murakhovskaya, Xiong, Wu (2024) Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs leads to performance drops in the FlipFlop experiment
finding: Gap 7. Ten LLMs, seven classification tasks. After a bare 'Are you sure?' challenge, models flip often and lose accuracy. All ten models lose accuracy.
numbers: Average flip rate 46%; average accuracy drop 17% (the FlipFlop effect). Seven of ten models lose 10+ points. Example drops on one 100-sample set: GPT-4 -8%, Claude V2 -34%.
quote: models flip their answers on average 46% of the time
limits: Classification tasks with a fixed answer; the challenge carries no new evidence by design. Not forecasting.
agent_relevance: Evidence-free pushback is a clean test of a bad update. Our S5 should log a flip with no new evidence as a failure.

source: Laban, Murakhovskaya, Xiong, Wu (2024) Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs leads to performance drops in the FlipFlop experiment (model and challenger breakdown)
finding: Flip rate and damage differ widely by model, challenger wording and task. Models flip more when initially wrong than right, yet flipping still costs net accuracy.
numbers: FlipFlop effect correlates with overall flip rate (about -0.78) and only moderately with initial accuracy (0.52). Best challenger gives about 3x the damage of the weakest. Task spread: LegalBench-CCQA about 8x the damage of Logical Fallacy. Command-XL effect only -1.3%, partly because its initial accuracy was low.
limits: Persona and authority challengers worked best. Per-model table cells came from a jumbled text extraction and are not quoted.
agent_relevance: Authority framing is a stronger push than plain doubt. Test S5 against persona pushback, not only 'are you sure'.

source: Laban, Murakhovskaya, Xiong, Wu (2024) Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs leads to performance drops in the FlipFlop experiment (fine-tuning mitigation)
finding: Gap 7. Fine-tuning Mistral-7b on synthetic multi-turn data where the model keeps correct answers under challenge cuts the damage. Single-task tuning does not generalise. The authors warn that a never-flip model is a trivial and bad fix.
numbers: Base FlipFlop effect -9.5 average; best tuned model (multi-task, multi-challenger, plus instruction data) -3.8, a 60% cut. On the hard subset still -12 to -13, less than half the base. Apologies fell from 60% to under 2%.
limits: One 7B model; fine-tuning, not a prompt. No test of retraction on a true defeater, so it does not show the sycophancy vs Belief-R trade-off is solved.
agent_relevance: Supports training or prompting on both cases: hold under empty pushback, move on real evidence. No single prompt covering both has been shown.

source: Xie, Zhang, Chen, Lou, Su (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: behavior of LLMs in knowledge conflicts (ICLR 2024)
finding: Gap 7 and updating on retrieved evidence. LLMs adopt external evidence that contradicts their stored knowledge when it is coherent and convincing. But when evidence for both sides is shown, they favour the side that matches their memory.
numbers: Models include ChatGPT, GPT-4, PaLM2, Llama2-7B/70B, Vicuna-7B/33B, Qwen-7B. GPT-4 memorisation ratio about 80% on the most popular entities. With counter-memory only, models are highly receptive.
quote: LLMs show a strong confirmation bias
limits: Question answering on facts, with machine-built counter-evidence. Not forecasting.
agent_relevance: Both failures live in one model: easy capture by coherent false evidence, and clinging to prior when evidence is mixed. S5 needs a weigh-both-sides step and a source-quality check.

source: Xie, Zhang, Chen, Lou, Su (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: behavior of LLMs in knowledge conflicts (ICLR 2024) (evidence counts and order)
finding: Models mostly follow the majority of evidence. Confirmation bias grows with more memory-aligned evidence even at a fixed ratio (1 of 2 vs 2 of 4). GPT-4 and Vicuna-33B cling to memory even when more pieces favour the counter-answer (ratio 1 of 3). Order of evidence also matters.
numbers: Evidence order changes answers by more than 5% for some models and over 30% for PaLM2 and Llama2-7B. An appendix line gives 38.2% for a mixed-evidence setting; context not fully checked, treat as approximate.
agent_relevance: Balance or shuffle evidence order in S5 and count evidence items by direction before moving the number.

source: Wei, Huang, Lu, Zhou, Le (2024) Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy in large language models
finding: Sycophancy rises with scale and instruction tuning on opinion tasks. A light fine-tune on synthetic data where truth does not depend on user opinion reduces it. Models agree with objectively wrong addition statements when the user does.
numbers: PaLM 8B to 62B: +19.8% repeating the user view; 62B to 540B: a further +10.0%. Flan-PaLM-8B repeats the user view 26.0% more often than PaLM-8B. After intervention: 4.7% (62B) to 8.8% (8B) fewer matches; largest drop 10.0% (Flan-cont-PaLM-62B). Benchmark changes about -1.6 to +0.6 on MMLU/BBH.
limits: PaLM family only; fine-tuning; opinion tasks and toy addition, not belief revision under real defeaters.
agent_relevance: Sycophancy is a trained-in pull toward the user. A scaffold step that restates the evidence without the user's stated view may help; not tested.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Gap 5. A ReAct agent team with Google search and a Python interpreter forecasts competitively with the Manifold crowd on live questions. Python is in the toolkit but was not ablated alone.
numbers: Brier: RTF median of 3 0.169, mean of 3 0.170, single sampled 0.180, Manifold crowd 0.172; accuracy 73.9% (mean) vs 73.8% crowd. Halawi et al. GPT-4o 0.177, plain GPT-4o 0.210, base-LM mean 0.218, GPT-3.5 0.261. Ensemble std 0.092 (RTF) vs 0.150 (base).
limits: Small Manifold question set (spring 2024); tools bundled, so the Python effect is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays partly open: a tools agent can match a crowd, but posterior arithmetic by code is not separately measured on realistic forecasts.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting (NeurIPS 2024) (ablations and sequential-update note)
finding: Without ReAct guidance the agent misuses tools; without a high/low agent split, one agent burns tokens on API schemas and times out. The authors note that a prompt asking the model to update its estimate sequentially can over- or under-weight by recency.
numbers: Ensembles help only if members are already calibrated: RTF 0.169 vs 0.180; base LMs 0.218 vs 0.210 (GPT-4o). Most base methods score worse than always guessing 0.5 (Brier 0.25), GPT-4o excepted.
limits: The recency remark is qualitative, not measured.
agent_relevance: Order-of-consideration effects are a risk for sequential S5 updates. Ask for an order-shuffled second pass and compare.

source: Falck, Wang, Holmes (2024) Is in-context learning in LLMs Bayesian? A martingale perspective (ICML 2024)
finding: Gap 9 (closest test found). A martingale test of Bayesian updating needs no outcomes: a Bayesian predictor's forecast should not drift predictably as missing data is filled in. Tested on synthetic exchangeable sequences. LLMs violate it at longer horizons.
numbers: Models: GPT-3 (2.7B, 170B), GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2-7B, Mistral-7B. Short horizons mostly pass; at longer horizons (m=2n) more frequent violations; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 deviate on natural-language Bernoulli tasks. GPT-3.5 sample variance 0.711 (95% CI 0.680-0.742), below the likelihood variance 1, which no reasonable Bayesian model gives.
limits: Synthetic coin and Gaussian data, no reasoning models. This is NOT the Augenblick-Rabin forecast-stream test; it is an analogue.
agent_relevance: A cheap outcome-free audit for S5: if forecasts drift predictably under resampling or no-info text, the update rule is incoherent. Gap 9 stays open for real forecast streams.

source: Falck, Wang, Holmes (2024) Is in-context learning in LLMs Bayesian? A martingale perspective (ICML 2024) (uncertainty scaling)
finding: Epistemic uncertainty in LLMs does not shrink with data the way a Bayesian's does. GPT-3.5 and Llama-2-7B shrink slower than Bayesian, and GPT-3.5 is over-confident in small samples. GPT-3-170B and Mistral-7B are closer.
numbers: Descriptive rates in figures; no extra headline number read from text.
limits: Same synthetic setting. Instruction-tuned models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4) adhere worse than base GPT-3-170B in the Bernoulli tests.
agent_relevance: Instruction tuning may cost update coherence. Fits the Qiu stall result. Not tested with forecasts.

source: Pratt, Blumberg, Carolino, Morris (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: Gap 6 and gap 1. On prediction-market events one basic prompt beat the market on plain Brier, and every strategy prompt (breakdown, base rates, both sides, personas, news API) made plain Brier worse. The authors trace this to a low-probability bias; a weighted Brier that scores yes and no events equally reverses the picture.
numbers: Plain Brier (validation): Human 0.1334, Basic 0.1221, Forecaster 0.1483, Breakdown 0.1895, Base Rates 0.1562, Both Sides 0.1553, Crowd 0.1706, News API 0.1235. Weighted Brier: Human 0.1746 best; Basic 0.1955; News API 0.1950; Breakdown 0.2053.
limits: Most events resolve No, so low guesses win plain Brier. One model family; no belief-updating step tested. Table columns re-read from a text extraction.
agent_relevance: Do not judge S5 on plain Brier on skewed questions; use a class-weighted score. Prompt-only extremising was not tested here.

source: Pratt, Blumberg, Carolino, Morris (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies? (negativity bias, reversed events)
finding: Asked about an event and about its reverse, the model's two probabilities add to well below 1. Strategy prompts raise the mean prediction, which hurts plain Brier on skewed data only because it moves away from the low guess.
numbers: Mean P(event) 0.2529 (Basic) vs 1 - P(reversed) 0.3965; human market 0.3280. Brier Basic 0.1221 vs 1-Reversed 0.1814.
limits: Sum of about 0.86 is my derivation from two quoted means.
agent_relevance: A complement check (ask both ways) is a cheap consistency test inside S5; it ties to Paleka's consistency checks.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs (model list and future work)
finding: Gap 4. Models tested: Gemma 2 (9B, 27B), Llama 3 (8B, 70B), Qwen 2.5 (7B, 32B), GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro. The authors list reasoning-trained models as untested future work.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 is cited only in the question whether Bayesian teaching extends 'to the recent generation of models that are explicitly trained to reason in words'. Text search for o1, o3, thinking found no reasoning-model result.
limits: So the claim that reasoning models still stall is unproven either way.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open. Include a reasoning model as one arm in our test.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench (re-searched for reasoning models)
finding: Gap 4. A text search of the current arXiv PDF for o1, o3, DeepSeek-R1 and 'reasoning model' found none.
numbers: No numbers. Absence in this version only; the live leaderboard may include newer models.
limits: Weak evidence of absence. Leaderboard site not opened.
agent_relevance: No benchmark opened here separates reasoning from non-reasoning models on updating.

source: Atanasov et al. (2020) Small steps to accuracy (retry of the primary PDF)
finding: Gap 8. The Wharton-hosted PDF again came back as a 1-page file, so the text could not be read. No independent reproduction was found in any source I could open.
limits: Attempt only. No later replication on Good Judgment Open or IARPA data found.

source: Rethinking the Role of Teams and Training in Geopolitical Forecasting (2025, Psychological Science), Europe PMC record
finding: Gap 10. The abstract says best-fit models include extraneous variables that substantially eliminated, reduced, and in some cases reversed the experimental effects of teaming and training. Latent traits tied to strategic responding separate superforecasters from others, so the underlying factors are hard to name.
numbers: No effect sizes in the abstract. Publisher page returned 403.
limits: Abstract only. It does not mention update size or frequency. Linking it to Atanasov's 29% step-size mediation is my inference.
agent_relevance: If training effects are inflated, the step-size mediation is also suspect. Treat step size as a marker until a manipulation test.

source: Joint search of Laban, Xie, Wei, Hsieh, Falck, Pratt, Qiu and ForecastBench: LLM step size
finding: Gap 2 and 3. None of these papers reports mean absolute update size or confirmation rate for an LLM forecaster, or a first-forecast vs final-forecast accuracy split.
numbers: Zero studies found measuring the human 0.20 step and 19% confirmation figures in an LLM.
limits: Absence within what I could open under a rate-limited search budget; not proof that no one measured it.
agent_relevance: Measure it ourselves; logging S5 steps gives it for free.

source: Joint reading: Laban (2024), Wilie (2024), Wei (2024) on sycophancy vs defeater retraction
finding: Gap 7. Fixes for sycophancy (Laban tuning, Wei synthetic data) are scored only where the right move is to hold. Belief-R scores only where the right move is to move. No paper tests both in one model, so a single prompt that improves both is unproven.
numbers: Laban: FlipFlop -9.5 to -3.8 after tuning. Wilie: Llama-3 70B BU 10.99 vs BM 92.09 (update vs maintain). An unconditional hold hurts update; an unconditional move hurts maintain.
limits: Cross-paper reading by me; different tasks and models.
agent_relevance: Score hold and retract rates separately in the scaffold test, not accuracy alone.
